The paper demonstrates that a small, high-refractive index dielectric particle can exhibit ultra-weak total scattering due to the excitation of an anapole mode.
The anapole mode arises from the destructive interference of electric and toroidal dipole moments in the particle.
The key conditions for observing the anapole mode and ultra-weak scattering are: a small size parameter (q < 1), a large refractive index (typically n > 5), and weak dissipation.
For a particle with n = 15.0116 and q = 0.3, the total scattering efficiency is about 3.5 times less than the Rayleigh scattering calculated by the formula.
The anapole mode corresponds to a global minimum in the total scattering efficiency, unlike the Kerker conditions which minimize differential scattering functions.
The Fano resonance is crucial for the anapole mode, as it arises from the destructive interference between the electric dipole and toroidal dipole moments.
Near the anapole mode, the scattering pattern becomes polarization-dependent and non-rotationally symmetric, in contrast to the scattering patterns observed at the Kerker conditions.
Materials like SiC, TiO2, and ceramics can satisfy the conditions for observing the anapole mode and ultra-weak scattering in the far-IR and RF frequency domains.

The anapole mode and ultra-weak scattering can be used for designing highly transparent optical materials, such as clusters of nanoparticles with strongly suppressed scattering effects in the extinction.
The physics behind the anapole mode in small, spherical dielectric particles is explained in a different way compared to previous work on scattering suppression in dielectric rods.
The paper highlights the importance of the Fano resonance in the context of the anapole mode, as it is crucial for the global minimum in the total scattering efficiency.
The paper demonstrates that the anapole mode can be observed even in the simple spherical case, provided the particle is sufficiently small and has a sufficiently high refractive index.
The Poynting vector distribution for the particle with n = 15.0116 and q = 0.3 shows a toroidal structure, indicating the presence of the anapole mode.
The distributions of electric and magnetic vectors inside the particle in mutually perpendicular planes confirm the toroidal symmetry of the anapole mode.
The paper emphasizes that the conditions for ultra-weak scattering to occur are different from the Rayleigh approximation, which is not valid in the vicinity of the anapole mode.
